newsitem.title: USA: U.S., North Korea end "constructive" missile talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S., North Korea end "constructive" missile talks.

text.p: The United States and North Korea concluded a second round of "constructive" talks about Pyongyang's missile programme on Friday, a U.S. official involved in the negotiations said.
Speaking on condition of anonymity, the official told reporters the two sides planned to meet again, perhaps this summer in New York.
"We believe that these three days of discussions were constructive," he said. "We believe that they provide a basis for further discussions, but I don't want to go into any of the details."
Previous talks were held in April 1996 in Berlin. A second round was to have been held in May in New York but was delayed at North Korea's request.
The official said food aid for North Korea had not been discussed and the talks were still in an early stage.
"We hope that North Korea will see value to themselves, as well as to international peace and security, of constraining their international missile activity," he said.
The official declined to provide details or figures about North Korea's missile programme.
According to South Korea, North Korea can produce about 100 ground-to-ground Scud B and C missiles a year. It has exported about 400 to the Middle East.
Seoul has said that Pyongyang exports about $500 million worth of Scud missiles a year and that weaponry exports between 1980 and 1993 accounted for about 30 percent of North Korea's total exports.
Independent experts say North Korea has been exporting to Iran and Syria plants and machinery for producing Scuds as well as technology for developing them.

The talks were held at the U.S. mission to the United Nations. The U.S. negotiators were headed by Robert Einhorn, deputy assistant secretary of state, and the North Korean team was led by Li Hyong-chol, director of American affairs at the North Korean Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
